title: Pay transparency before recruitment
summary: Directive 2023/970 requires information on starting pay and prohibits questions about previous salaries. Publishing pay in the job advert is one option, not the only permitted way to communicate it.
body: Article 5 requires applicants to receive the starting pay or pay range, based on objective, gender-neutral criteria, along with the relevant collective agreement provisions. The information must allow informed negotiation, for example through the job advert or before the interview. Prepare a documented pay range for each role.

The text prohibits asking about pay history and requires gender-neutral job adverts and titles. Remove these questions from forms and interview scripts. Article 34 sets the transposition deadline at 7 juin 2026. For the Belgian situation, see the entry eu-transparence-salariale-transposition-belge. This deadline alone does not establish that a Belgian law applies to all private employers.
source: Council of the European Union · consilium.europa.eu

title: Pay transparency: Belgian transposition incomplete
summary: Sources consulted as of 30 septembre 2026 do not establish that general federal transposition for the private sector is complete. Belgium’s request for six months concerned infringement proceedings and did not change the European deadline.
body: In his reply of 15 juin 2026, point 03.10 of the proceedings, the Minister of Employment confirms that work is continuing and no precise timetable can be announced. He distinguishes a request to suspend the infringement procedure deadline for six months from an extension of the transposition deadline.

The minister notes that Belgian legislation on discrimination and the pay gap remains applicable. He explains that, in principle, an untransposed directive does not directly create obligations between private parties. Do not present this delay as permission to discriminate or extend this analysis to public employers.

An analysis dated 17 septembre 2026 still reports no federal draft legislation and highlights the possible effects of interpreting national law in line with the directive: https://pkfbofidi.com/loontransparantie-belgie-zonder-omzettingswet/. Federated entities have notified partial measures, but these do not establish full federal transposition. Before stating that a new Belgian obligation applies to a client, check the published text and its scope.

title: Transparent and predictable working conditions
summary: Directive 2019/1152 requires written employment information and guarantees of predictability. Its minimum requirements must be read alongside the Belgian transposition rules.
body: Articles 3 to 5 require, among other things, the identity of the parties, the role, workplace, start date, duration where applicable, pay and working hours. The European baseline requires the main information to be provided by the seventh calendar day and the rest within a month. Electronic formats must allow access, saving and printing, with proof of transmission or receipt.

Articles 9, 10 and 13 regulate restrictions on holding multiple jobs, assignments with unpredictable schedules and free mandatory training. For recruitment in Belgium, apply national deadlines, including individual information from the first day, as described in the entry eu-information-embauche-belgique. The European cap on probationary periods does not authorise the inclusion of a probation clause in Belgium.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: Belgium: information to provide when employment starts
summary: The FPS Employment explains Belgium’s transposition of Directive 2019/1152 through the law of 7 octobre 2022. Prepare individual information for the first day of work.
body: Provide, among other things, the parties, workplace, role, start date, end date or duration of a fixed-term contract, pay components and schedule information. Collective details, including applicable collective agreements and the competent joint body, are generally set out in the work regulations.

The contract or a separate document may be used. Electronic delivery requires a document that can be accessed, saved and printed, and proof of sending or receipt must be retained. Individual information must reach the worker no later than the first day. Communicate changes no later than when they take effect, except for simple changes to the texts referenced. The law was published on 31 octobre 2022.

owner.name: SPF Emploi, Travail et Concertation sociale

title: Recruitment without racial or ethnic discrimination
summary: Directive 2000/43 prohibits racial or ethnic discrimination in access to employment. Selection criteria and recruitment conditions are explicitly covered.
body: Articles 2 and 3 cover direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and instructions to discriminate, in both the public and private sectors. Review adverts, screening criteria and client requests to prevent them from excluding applicants on grounds of racial or ethnic origin.

Article 4 permits different treatment only under the strict conditions of a genuine and determining occupational requirement, with a legitimate objective and a proportionate requirement. A general customer preference is not enough to establish such a requirement. Article 3, paragraph 2, distinguishes this framework from nationality, entry and residence rules. Check the right to work separately from the applicant’s origin.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: Age, disability and beliefs: equality in recruitment
summary: Directive 2000/78 protects applicants against discrimination based on beliefs, age, disability or sexual orientation. Provide the reasonable accommodation needed for selection.
body: The Commission notes that the prohibitions cover selection criteria, recruitment, training and employment conditions. They also cover indirect discrimination, harassment and instructions to discriminate. Use criteria related to the job’s tasks and keep a record of the professional reasons for decisions.

Article 5 requires reasonable accommodation to give people with disabilities access to employment, unless this imposes a disproportionate burden. Assess specific adjustments to interviews, tests or the role. Consider available support before concluding that the burden is excessive. Protection covers public and private employment. The directive was published on 2 décembre 2000.

title: Gender equality in selection and pay
summary: Directive 2006/54 prohibits sex discrimination in recruitment and requires equal pay for equal work or work of equal value. Pregnancy cannot justify unfavourable treatment.
body: Article 14 covers access to employment and selection criteria at all levels. Article 2 includes sexual harassment and less favourable treatment related to pregnancy or maternity leave. Remove sex-based criteria without legal justification and assess the skills needed for the role.

Article 4 covers all elements of pay and the job classifications used to set them. Compare roles using the same criteria for women and men. The exception in Article 14, paragraph 2, requires a characteristic that constitutes a genuine and determining occupational requirement, with a legitimate aim and a proportionate requirement.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: Fixed-term contracts: equal treatment and renewals
summary: Directive 1999/70 protects fixed-term workers against unjustified differences in treatment and abusive renewals. Check Belgian law for the specific limits on successive contracts.
body: The Commission explains that a contract being temporary does not in itself justify less favourable conditions than those of a comparable permanent worker. Any difference must rest on objective grounds. Check the advertised benefits and the conditions offered for the fixed-term contract.

To prevent abuse, Member States must provide one or more measures: objective grounds for renewal, a maximum total duration or a maximum number of renewals. The directive does not set a uniform number of fixed-term contracts allowed throughout the Union. Check the sequence of contracts before offering a new fixed-term contract. The text, published on 10 July 1999, also covers seasonal workers within its scope.

title: Part-time work: rights and access to jobs
summary: Directive 97/81 prohibits less favourable treatment solely because a worker works part-time. Distinguish proportionate entitlements from unjustified exclusions.
body: Clause 4 of the framework agreement prohibits less favourable conditions than those of a comparable full-time worker, unless justified on objective grounds. The pro rata principle applies where appropriate. State the proposed working arrangement and check how pay and benefits are calculated.

Clause 5 calls on employers, where possible, to consider requests to move between full-time and part-time work and to provide information on available jobs. A worker refusing to change their working arrangement is not, in itself, a valid reason for dismissal. These European requirements, published on 20 January 1998, do not replace the Belgian formalities specific to part-time contracts and working schedules.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: Under 18: access to work and working hours
summary: Directive 94/33 protects young workers, regardless of their contract type. Check age, compulsory schooling requirements and job risks before hiring a minor.
body: Articles 1 to 4 prohibit child labour, with limited exceptions to be implemented nationally. Under the text, an adolescent is at least 15, under 18 and no longer subject to compulsory full-time schooling. A European exception does not remove the need to check the corresponding authorisation in Belgium.

In the consolidated version of 26 July 2019, Articles 8 to 12 generally provide for adolescents to work 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week, with 12 consecutive hours of daily rest and a break of at least 30 minutes when work exceeds 4 and a half hours. Night work is restricted. Articles 6 and 7 require a prior risk assessment and prohibit certain hazardous tasks. Check the more protective Belgian rules and the specific exemptions.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: GDPR: CVs, references and recruitment tests
summary: The Data Protection Authority explains how to apply the GDPR to recruitment. Collect only data needed for the role and set rules for references and automated decisions.
body: Questionnaires and interviews must respect the candidate's privacy. Do not routinely collect health data or criminal records information. The Data Protection Authority notes that consent alone does not authorise the processing of criminal records data covered by Article 10 of Regulation 2016/679.

For reference checks, the Data Protection Authority requires prior information and freely given authorisation specifying the people to be consulted, the data, the reasons and the period. Refusal must not automatically end the selection process. A reference listed on a CV may count as consent.

A hiring decision must not be based solely on an automated test with a significant effect, unless a legal exception and the applicable safeguards apply. Provide for human review and the opportunity for candidates to express their views. For CVs retained after selection, document the purpose, legal basis, necessary retention period and information given to the candidate, in accordance with Articles 5, 6 and 13 of the GDPR. This page sets no universal retention period. The GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018.

title: EU Blue Card: recruiting highly qualified workers
summary: Directive 2021/1883 makes it easier to recruit highly qualified workers from third countries. Check qualifications, the offer and the Belgian salary threshold applicable to the place of employment.
body: The Commission sets out the requirements of the revised scheme, which entered into force on 27 November 2021: a contract or binding offer for at least six months and higher qualifications or accepted professional skills. The salary threshold set nationally is between 1 and 1,6 times the average gross annual salary. This is neither a maximum salary nor a uniform Belgian amount.

Professional experience may be recognised in some cases, particularly in IT. After 12 months in the first Member State, simplified mobility to another Member State is possible. This requires the procedures specified by the host country. When hiring in Belgium, check the permit, regional conditions and threshold in force on the application date before guaranteeing a start date.

title: Single permit: new European framework
summary: Directive 2024/1233 revises the single permit procedure and strengthens the rights of workers from non-EU countries. Its transposition deadline was 21 May 2026.
body: Article 5 requires a decision within 90 days of a complete application, including the labour market assessment. Article 8 allows an exceptional extension of 30 days, duly justified by the complexity of the case. A request for additional documents may pause the deadline. If the employer submits the application, it must inform the applicant of its progress and outcome.

Article 11 provides for changes of employer subject to national conditions and protects certain periods of unemployment. Articles 18 to 20 set the transposition deadline at 21 May 2026 and repeal Directive 2011/98 on 22 May 2026. These European deadlines do not authorise anyone to start work. Check the Belgian procedure that actually applies and the residence and work authorisations before employment begins.
source: Publications Office of the European Union · eur-lex.europa.eu

title: Working time: European rest requirements and limits
summary: Directive 2003/88 sets minimum rest periods and limits on working time. When drafting a Belgian job offer, also check national and sector-specific rules.
body: The Commission recalls the average limit of 48 hours per week, including overtime, and minimum rest periods of 11 consecutive hours in each 24-hour period and 24 hours per week in addition to daily rest. A break is required when work exceeds 6 hours, and paid annual leave must be at least 4 weeks.

The average is calculated over the legally permitted reference period. Exceptions and specific arrangements exist, particularly in transport. These requirements, from the text published on 18 November 2003, do not allow 48 hours to be presented as normal working time in Belgium. Check the advertised schedule, rest periods and night work rules before publishing.

title: Platform work: employment status and algorithms
summary: Directive 2024/2831 provides for a rebuttable presumption of an employment relationship and regulates algorithmic management. As of 30 September 2026, its transposition deadline is still ahead.
body: The Commission explains that Member States must make reclassification easier when the declared status does not match the work actually performed. Before offering assignments on a self-employed basis, examine how the platform organises the work in practice, particularly task allocation, pricing and oversight. The directive does not automatically turn all service providers into employees.

The text strengthens transparency about algorithms and the ability to challenge decisions affecting working conditions. It also provides for better traceability of platform work. The directive was published on 11 November 2024; transposition is required by 2 December 2026 at the latest, under Article 29. Distinguish these European requirements from Belgian rules already in force.

title: Recruitment AI: high-risk classification
summary: Annex III to Regulation 2024/1689 covers AI tools for targeting job advertisements, screening applications and assessing candidates. Classify each use before choosing or deploying a tool.
body: Point 4 of Annex III covers recruitment and selection, as well as certain decisions on working conditions, promotion, termination and worker assessment. This category applies to recruiters in all sectors; it is not limited to IT companies.

Article 6 provides for limited exceptions for certain uses that pose no significant risk; an Annex III system that performs profiling remains high-risk. Ask the provider for its written justification of the classification. The text is reproduced by the Commission's official service: https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6. The timeline changed in July 2026; consult eu-ia-calendrier-omnibus-2026 before presenting high-risk obligations as already applicable.
source: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk · ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu

owner.name: Parlement européen et Conseil de l’Union européenne

title: High-risk AI: obligations for employers using it
summary: Article 26 of the AI Act defines the obligations of professional users of high-risk AI. Prepare human oversight, information for affected people and traceability in line with the revised timeline.
body: An employer using the system must follow the provider's instructions, appoint competent people with the necessary authority to oversee the tool, and monitor its operation. Where the employer controls the input data, that data must be relevant and sufficiently representative. Article 26 requires logs under its control to be kept for an appropriate period of at least six months, unless another applicable rule provides otherwise.

Inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using the system at work; also inform people subject to a decision assisted by an Annex III system. Put alert procedures in place and carry out a GDPR impact assessment where required. For Annex III recruitment tools, high-risk obligations are postponed until 2 December 2027 under the timeline presented in eu-ia-calendrier-omnibus-2026.
source: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk · ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu

owner.name: Parlement européen et Conseil de l’Union européenne

title: AI Act: timeline changed in July 2026
summary: The Commission confirms that the AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026. Rules for high-risk systems listed in Annex III will apply from 2 December 2027.
body: The official page, updated on 31 July 2026, distinguishes two deadlines: 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems, including recruitment, and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems built into Annex I products. Update internal schedules that still use August 2026 for the high-risk obligations of selection tools.

The package also simplifies AI literacy provisions and certain administrative obligations. Avoid reusing guides based solely on the original 2024 version without checking them. Postponing high-risk rules does not suspend the GDPR or the bans on discrimination that apply to recruitment.
